relative_claims.statement: ERM fails on target despite near-perfect source accuracy
relative_claims.verbatim: The results in Table 1 (implementation details in Appendix A.1) show that ERM is unable to learn the slab feature, as evident by poor generalization to the target domain, despite very good performance on the source domains.

relative_claims.statement: Unconditional DM (DANN, MMD, CORAL), conditional DM (CDANN, C-MMD, C-CORAL) and RandMatch all fail to learn the stable slab feature
relative_claims.verbatim: We also show that methods based on learning invariant representations by unconditional (DANN, MMD, CORAL) and conditional distribution matching (CDANN, C-MMD, C-CORAL), and matching same-class inputs (Random-Match) (Motiian et al., 2017) fail to learn the stable slab feature.

relative_claims.statement: CDM methods fail to generalize to target even though slab distribution is similar across source domains
relative_claims.verbatim: However, the slab dataset has similar distribution of stable feature (slabs) across the source domains, yet the CDM algorithms fail to generalize to the target domain.

relative_claims.statement: CDM methods can fail empirically even with equal stable-feature distribution across domains
relative_claims.verbatim: This shows that the CDM methods can empirically fail even when there is an equal distribution of stable features across domains.

relative_claims.statement: Matching representations of cross-domain points with the same slab value (PerfectMatch) substantially improves out-of-domain accuracy, to 78%
relative_claims.magnitude: target accuracy 78% (Table 1: 77.8); no explicit margin stated in text. Implied by Table 1: +20.2 over ERM (57.6), +13.1 over best baseline C-CORAL (64.7) -- these differences are computed, not stated.
relative_claims.verbatim: We do so by minimizing the ℓ_2 -norm of the representations for data points from different domains that share the same slab value (details of the PerfectMatch method in Section 4.3). The results improve substantially: out-of-domain accuracy is now 78%.
relative_claims.where: Section 3.2, paragraph starting 'How can we ensure that a model learns the stable, generalizable feature x2?'

perfmatch_description.one_line: PerfMatch (PerfectMatch) adds an l2 penalty between representations Phi(x) of cross-domain input pairs that share the same slab id, i.e. the same value of the causal/stable feature (ground-truth 'object' matches); the paper says such object information is not always available in practice (it is an oracle-style match that the slab simulation provides; MatchDG is proposed to approximate it).

evidence.verbatim: For RandMatch (Motiian et al., 2017) and PerfMatch, we use ℓ_2 distance for dist in (Eq: 3).

For the PerfectMatch algorithm, the match function Ω accepts two data points across domains with the same slab id as valid matches (the slab id corresponds to the value of the causal feature: two inputs with the same slab id have similar causal features).
The match function Ω in the RandMatch algorithm is defined as randomly matching any two data points across domains with the same class label.
We do so by minimizing the ℓ_2 -norm of the representations for data points from different domains that share the same slab value (details of the PerfectMatch method in Section 4.3).
When object information is available, Eq. (3) provides a loss objective to build a classifer using causal features.
However, object information is not always available, and in many datasets there may not be a perfect "counterfactual" match based on same object across domains.
We propose matching-based algorithms when base objects are observed (e.g., through data augmentation) and approximate the objective when objects are not observed (MatchDG).
